content: The relationship between infection prevalence and intensity has been studied, but certain parameters, such as hypoproteinaemia, which are associated with heavy parasitic infections, remain difficult to measure accurately. There is a lack of high-quality epidemiological data to support these associations. Research has been conducted to explore the impact of parasitic infections on school performance, cognitive abilities, and athletic performance, often through chemotherapy interventions. However, distinguishing the effects of these infections from other confounding factors, such as microand macronutrient deficiencies, is challenging. Schistosomiasis is endemic in 76 tropical and subtropical countries. Schistosoma mansoni is found in 54 countries, while Schistosoma haematobium is present in 55. Schistosoma japonicum continues to pose a significant public health burden in the Philippines, China, and parts of Indonesia, despite ongoing control programs. Globally, approximately 800 million people are at risk of schistosomiasis, with an estimated 200 million infected. Among these, 160 million live in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where 110 million are infected with S. haematobium. Schistosomiasis causes 150,000–280,000 deaths annually in SSA and leads to severe disability in about 20 million individuals. Chronic schistosomiasis can result in portal hypertension and organomegaly in 5–8% of untreated cases and is strongly associated with liver and bladder cancers. S. haematobium infection is particularly severe, causing hydronephrosis, renal failure, and bladder cancer. Women with urinary schistosomiasis are at increased risk of HIV infection. Over 80% of the global burden of schistosomiasis is concentrated in SSA. In Latin America and the Caribbean, schistosomiasis (S. mansoni) is prevalent in Brazil, Suriname, and Venezuela, with 25 million people at risk and 1–3 million infected. However, the true burden of schistosomiasis is likely underestimated. For most helminth infections, including schistosomiasis, infection does not always equate to disease. Validated indicators of schistosome-related morbidity are scarce. In urinary schistosomiasis, gross haematuria is an early sign of morbidity, but assessing morbidity for S. mansoni and S. japonicum is more complex. Many clinical manifestations of schistosomiasis are nonspecific and may overlap with other conditions, such as malaria or other helminth infections, which often coexist with schistosomiasis. Human liver fluke infections, caused by food-borne trematodes such as Opisthorchis viverrini, Opisthorchis felineus, and Clonorchis sinensis, remain significant public health concerns, particularly in Asia. Chronic infections with O. viverrini and C. sinensis are strongly linked to cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer). C. sinensis is widespread in China, Korea, and Vietnam, while O. viverrini is endemic in Southeast Asia, including Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and central Vietnam. Approximately 35 million people are infected with C. sinensis globally, with up to 15 million cases in China alone. Another 10 million individuals are infected with O. viverrini in Thailand and Laos. Liver fluke infections are associated with hepatobiliary diseases, including hepatomegaly, cholangitis, periportal fibrosis, cholecystitis, gallstones, and cholangiocarcinoma. In Khon Kaen, Thailand, the highest incidence of liver cancer globally has been reported, largely due to liver fluke infections. Liver and bile duct cancers, end-stage consequences of liver fluke disease, rank among the top causes of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) in Thailand. Taenia solium is endemic in Latin America, large parts of Asia (including China and the Indian subcontinent), Eastern Europe, and most of Africa. Imported cases are also reported in developed countries due to immigration and tourism. The T. solium taeniasis/cysticercosis complex involves two distinct clinical entities. Taeniasis, the intestinal infection caused by the adult tapeworm, has low morbidity but serves as the primary source of cysticercosis in humans and pigs. Cysticercosis, caused by the larval stage of the parasite, is a major cause of seizure disorders worldwide (neurocysticercosis or NCC) and leads to economic losses due to infected pork. In endemic areas of Latin America, NCC accounts for approximately 30% of all seizure disorders. Subarachnoid NCC is associated with intracranial hypertension and mortality. Control of S. japonicum and cestode infections is complicated by their zoonotic nature, with animals such as cattle, buffalo, rodents, dogs, sheep, and pigs acting as reservoirs for human transmission. In China, integrated control efforts for S. japonicum include removing bovines from snail-infested grasslands, providing tap water, and implementing intensive health education. Despite the proven efficacy of praziquantel (PZQ) for schistosomiasis and cestode infections, there is a need for improved drugs, combination regimens, and dosage studies to enhance efficacy and reduce transmission risks. Human helminthiases are characterized by long-lasting infections, often involving multiple helminth species (polyparasitism). This phenomenon arises from shared ecological and environmental factors, infection routes, host exposures, and behavioral, sociological, and economic conditions. Polyparasitism may exacerbate morbidity beyond the sum of single-species infections and increase susceptibility to other infections, such as malaria or HIV, due to the immunosuppressive effects of helminth infections. Efforts are underway to understand the immunological interactions between coexisting parasites and their impact on resistance, susceptibility, and clinical outcomes. Co-infections are also shifting control strategies from single-drug treatments to integrated approaches targeting multiple neglected tropical diseases, such as onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, soil-transmitted helminthiases, and schistosomiasis. The Disease Reference Group on Helminth Infections (DRG4) consists of 13 experts from research institutions, international organizations, and governmental bodies. The group prioritizes research on helminth infections, including onchocerciasis, lymphatic filariasis, soil-transmitted helminthiases, schistosomiasis, food-borne trematodiases, and taeniasis/cysticercosis. Key research areas include epidemiology, diagnostic tools, drug resistance, vaccine development, and access to treatment. The group emphasizes the need for sustainable control measures, advocacy, and capacity building in endemic countries.
